context.heading: Mending a torn net
context.body: Paul answers schisma ("divisions") with katartizō ("united"), a verb used for mending fishing nets (Mark 1:19) and for setting a broken bone. He is not asking the Corinthians to hold identical opinions on everything. He wants a torn fabric repaired, so the church can work as one body again.

context.heading: Patrons, teachers and status
context.body: In Roman Corinth people gained honor by attaching themselves to a powerful patron or a famous teacher, and rival orators drew loyal followings. Some believers seem to have treated Paul, Apollos and Cephas the same way, raising their own standing through their chosen leader. The cry "I follow Christ" may have been one more party slogan rather than a humble answer.

context.heading: The trigger of a trap
context.body: Skandalon ("stumbling block") first meant the stick that springs a trap, then anything that trips a person up. For many Jews a crucified Messiah was a contradiction, since Deuteronomy 21:23 says anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse. Paul does not soften it. The very thing that trips people is the heart of his message (Galatians 3:13).

theology.title: God chooses the overlooked
theology.body: God's pattern here is old. He chose a small, enslaved Israel rather than a great empire (Deuteronomy 7:7), younger sons over elder ones, and a shepherd boy over his brothers. In Corinth He chose people with little education, power or pedigree (v. 26). His choices remove every ground for boasting, so the glory goes to Him alone (Jeremiah 9:23–24, quoted in v. 31).

theology.title: Christ is our wisdom
theology.body: Paul does not just say Christ gives wisdom. Christ became for us wisdom from God: righteousness, holiness and redemption (v. 30). Everything needed to stand before God is found in a person, not a philosophy. And the faithful God who called them will keep them blameless to the end (vv. 8–9).

application.title: Check your fan club
application.body: It is easy to build an identity around a favorite preacher, podcast or author, and to size up other believers by whether they follow the same voice. Paul's reply is blunt: no teacher was crucified for you. Gratitude for good teachers is right; tribal loyalty to them tears the church.
application.question: Whose name do you reach for first when you want to prove you are on the right side?

application.title: Your credentials are not your standing
application.body: Corinth ran on pedigree, connections and polish, and so does most of modern life. Verse 26 is a quiet relief: God did not choose you for your credentials, so losing them cannot unchoose you. The only boast left is in what He has done.
application.question: What would change in how you work this week if your worth were not riding on your performance?

application.title: Do not polish the cross
application.body: In verse 17 Paul refuses to dress up the gospel to make it sound impressive. We can be tempted to lead with the respectable parts of faith and stay quiet about a crucified Savior. The power sits in the part that sounds foolish.
application.question: Which part of the gospel do you tend to skip with skeptical friends, and why?

context.heading: No showman's speech
context.body: Hyperochē means "superiority" or "excellence", and paired with logos it describes lofty, showy speech. Sophists traveled from city to city dazzling crowds with eloquence and charging for it. Paul deliberately refused that style when he arrived in Corinth (Acts 18:1–5), so no one could mistake a speaker's skill for the power of God.

context.heading: An honest admission of fear
context.body: Paul says he came "in weakness and fear, and with much trembling". Acts 18:9–10 records the Lord telling him in a vision at Corinth, "Do not be afraid", which suggests real anxiety. Orators were expected to project confidence and command the room. Paul admits the opposite and treats it as no embarrassment.

context.heading: A mystery now made public
context.body: In Corinth the mystery cults offered secret rites to a select inner circle. Paul's mystērion ("mystery") is different. It is God's plan, set before time and hidden until He chose to reveal it, and now openly proclaimed to everyone (Romans 16:25–26). The secret is not for insiders; it is the cross, announced in the street.

theology.title: The Spirit knows God from within
theology.body: Only a person's own spirit knows his inner thoughts, and only God's Spirit knows God's (v. 11). The Spirit is no mere force; He shares God's own knowledge from the inside. The chapter is a clear window on the Trinity: the Father's hidden plan, the crucified Lord of glory, and the Spirit who reveals both.

theology.title: The Lord of glory was crucified
theology.body: Verse 8 calls the crucified Jesus "the Lord of glory", language the Old Testament uses for God Himself (Psalm 24:7–10). Paul sets the highest divine title beside the most shameful death. The rulers of this age thought they were removing a troublemaker; they were crucifying the King of glory and unknowingly fulfilling God's plan.

application.title: Stop waiting to sound impressive
application.body: Paul refused to win people by sounding clever. Many believers stay silent because they fear they cannot explain things well, while others hide behind polished words. Plain, honest testimony about Christ is what God tends to use.
application.question: Where are you waiting to feel more competent before you speak about Jesus?

application.title: When faith baffles people you love
application.body: Verse 14 explains why a coworker or relative can hear the gospel and find it absurd. That is not proof you failed or that they are foolish; spiritual things are spiritually discerned. It frees you to keep loving them without needing to win every argument.
application.question: Whose confusion about your faith have you been treating as your personal failure?

application.title: Learning the mind of Christ
application.body: "We have the mind of Christ" is not a claim to know everything. It means believers can learn to think about money, people and suffering the way Jesus does, through the Scriptures the Spirit gave. That mind grows by steady exposure, not by osmosis.
application.question: Which of your strongest opinions has never actually been tested against how Jesus thinks?

context.heading: Made of flesh, led by flesh
context.body: Paul uses two related words. In verse 1 the Corinthians are sarkinos, "made of flesh", a description of infancy. In verse 3 they are sarkikos ("worldly" or "fleshly"), which is a charge: they are acting on mere human instinct. Their jealousy and quarreling showed Spirit-filled people living as if the Spirit made no difference.

context.heading: The head craftsman
context.body: An architektōn ("expert builder") was the master craftsman who ran a building project on site. Corinth's public buildings often carried the carved names of the wealthy donors who paid for them. Paul laid the foundation, but the foundation itself is Jesus Christ. No worker gets his name chiseled on God's building.

context.heading: Assayed by fire
context.body: Dokimazō ("prove" or "test") was used for assaying metal in fire to show whether it was genuine. Gold and silver survive the flames; wood, hay and straw do not. "The Day" is the Lord's day of judgment. Paul is weighing the quality of believers' work, especially leaders' work, not whether the builder himself is saved (v. 15).

theology.title: Only God gives growth
theology.body: Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God made it grow (v. 6). The Old Testament pictures God's people as His vineyard and planting (Isaiah 5:1–7; 61:3), and here the same Gardener is at work. Leaders matter as servants, but they cannot manufacture life. Every real change in a person is God's doing.

theology.title: A temple made of people
theology.body: Israel's temple was where God's glory dwelt (1 Kings 8:10–11). Now the gathered church is that temple, and the "you" in verses 16–17 is plural. The God who once filled a building lives among His people by His Spirit. That is why tearing a church apart is so serious: it damages God's own dwelling.

application.title: Build with what survives fire
application.body: Two people can serve in the same church for twenty years, one building with gold and one with straw, and look identical from the outside. The fire tests motives, not just activity. Applause and self-promotion burn fast.
application.question: If your service this year were tested by fire, what would actually be left standing?

application.title: Leaders are farmhands
application.body: In verse 7 Paul calls himself and Apollos nothing compared with the God who gives growth. That cuts both ways: do not idolize a pastor, and do not crush one with expectations only God can meet. Pastors plant and water; they do not control the harvest.
application.question: What are you expecting from a church leader that only God can give you?

application.title: You inherit the whole family
application.body: Paul ends with a staggering inventory: Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, present and future all belong to you, and you belong to Christ. You do not need to pick a team. Every faithful teacher is a gift to you.
application.question: Which teacher or tradition have you dismissed that God may have given you as a gift?

context.heading: "Already kings"
context.body: "Already you have become rich! You have begun to reign" is heavy irony. Some Corinthians seem to have acted as if the full blessings of the age to come had already arrived, leaving no room for suffering or weakness. Scholars often call this an over-realized view of the end. Paul wishes they did reign, so the apostles could share it.

context.heading: The scrapings of the world
context.body: Perikatharma means what is scoured off in cleaning, the filth left behind. Greek writers also used it for the lowest of people, sometimes outcasts driven from a city to carry off its curse. Peripsēma ("refuse") is a similar word for scrapings. Paul accepts the worst labels Corinth could give, because that is what following a crucified Lord looked like.

context.heading: Many tutors, one father
context.body: A paidagōgos ("guardian") was usually a household slave who walked a boy to school, watched his conduct and disciplined him. A child might have several over the years but only one father. Paul planted the church in Corinth, which gave him a father's bond and responsibility that later teachers, however helpful, could not replace.

theology.title: The Lord who weighs hearts
theology.body: Paul's conscience is clear, yet that does not acquit him; the Lord is his judge (v. 4). God will bring hidden things to light and expose the motives of hearts (v. 5; compare 1 Samuel 16:7). That is sobering and freeing. God's verdict is the only one that finally counts, and it includes His praise for the faithful.

theology.title: Everything is received
theology.body: "What do you have that you did not receive?" (v. 7) is a one-line theology of grace. Every ability and opportunity comes from God, as Israel was warned not to say "my power has gained me this wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:17–18). God is the giver behind every good thing, so boasting is not only rude. It takes credit that belongs to Him.

application.title: Step out of the jury box
application.body: In verse 3 Paul does not even judge himself. Constant self-scrutiny and checking others' approval can be pride turned inward. Faithfulness with what God entrusted, leaving the verdict to Him, is far lighter.
application.question: Whose verdict on you are you replaying in your head more than God's?

application.title: Trace your strengths backward
application.body: Take your proudest achievement and trace it back: the health, family, teachers and timing you did not create. Verse 7 does not shrink effort; it moves the credit. Gratitude replaces swagger.
application.question: Which strength of yours do you quietly treat as self-made?

application.title: Someone is already copying you
application.body: In verse 16 Paul says "imitate me", and his life was hungry, homeless, insulted and patient. Faith passes down mostly by watching, not by lectures. Someone near you is already learning from how you handle insult and inconvenience.
application.question: If someone younger copied your reactions this week, what would they learn about following Jesus?

context.heading: A union even Rome condemned
context.body: Roman law forbade a man to marry his stepmother, and Roman writers treated such unions as scandalous. "His father's wife" probably means his stepmother, and the present tense suggests an ongoing relationship. Paul does not address the woman, so she was probably not a believer. The church was tolerating what its pagan neighbors condemned.

context.heading: Inflated instead of grieving
context.body: Physioō ("proud") means to puff up or inflate, like a bellows. Paul uses it six times in this letter (4:6, 18, 19; 5:2; 8:1; 13:4) and only once anywhere else (Colossians 2:18). Whether the Corinthians were proud of their tolerance or simply proud in spite of the scandal, they were swollen with self-regard when they should have been mourning.

context.heading: Handed over to Satan
context.body: Olethros means "ruin" or "destruction". Handing someone "to Satan" probably means putting him outside the fellowship, back into the realm where Satan holds sway (compare 1 Timothy 1:20). Interpreters debate whether "the flesh" means his sinful nature or his body bearing consequences. Either way the goal is rescue: "so that his spirit may be saved".

theology.title: A holy God among His people
theology.body: Paul ends by quoting Deuteronomy's refrain, "Expel the wicked man from among you" (v. 13; Deuteronomy 17:7). The holy God who dwelt with Israel now dwells in the church, which makes holiness a shared matter, not only a private one. Discipline guards the place where God lives.

theology.title: Judgment that aims at rescue
theology.body: Even the hardest step in this chapter has salvation as its goal. God disciplines as a Father, to bring wanderers home and share His holiness (Hebrews 12:10–11). Some think 2 Corinthians 2:5–8 shows this man later restored, though many scholars think that passage concerns someone else.

application.title: Looking away is not love
application.body: The Corinthians thought silence was generous; Paul calls it arrogance. Staying quiet about a friend's destructive pattern can be more about protecting your comfort than caring for them.
application.question: Who needs you to say something hard that you have been filing under "not my business"?

application.title: Judge inside, not outside
application.body: Paul never told believers to avoid immoral unbelievers; that would mean leaving the world. Christians often reverse his order, scolding outsiders while excusing sin among their own. Paul says deal honestly with the church and leave outsiders to God.
application.question: Are you harder on the sins of people outside the church than on the sins of your own circle?

application.title: Small leaven, whole batch
application.body: A little yeast works through the whole lump. A habit excused as minor, a bit of dishonesty at work or a private screen habit, rarely stays small. Christ's sacrifice is both the reason and the power to clear it out.
application.question: What "small" thing are you keeping that is quietly spreading into everything else?

context.heading: Courts that favored the powerful
context.body: Civil lawsuits in Roman cities were mostly brought by the wealthy and well-connected, and judges tended to favor people of higher status. A suit could also be a way to shame a rival in public. So believers suing one another probably meant richer members using the system against poorer ones, in front of unbelieving magistrates.

context.heading: You have already lost
context.body: Hēttēma means "loss" or "defeat". The moment believers drag each other to court, Paul says, they have already lost, whatever the verdict. Winning the case still leaves a defeated church. Better to be wronged or cheated, echoing Jesus' teaching about the one who would sue you for your tunic (Matthew 5:39–40).

context.heading: A slogan turned on its head
context.body: "Everything is permissible for me" was probably a Corinthian slogan, perhaps Paul's teaching on freedom pushed too far. Paul answers with a pun. Exestin ("it is permissible") and exousiazō ("to be mastered") share a root to do with authority. Using your right to do anything can leave you under the authority of something else.

theology.title: The body matters to God
theology.body: Many Greeks treated the body as a shell the soul would one day escape. Scripture disagrees: God made the body good (Genesis 1:31), the Son took on flesh, and God raised Jesus bodily and will raise us too (v. 14). A God who redeems bodies cares what we do with them.

theology.title: Joined to the Lord
theology.body: Paul quotes Genesis 2:24, "the two will become one flesh", to show sex is never merely physical. Then he says the believer united to the Lord is "one with Him in spirit" (v. 17). Scripture often pictures God as His people's husband (Hosea 2:19–20). Union with Christ makes sexual sin a betrayal of a covenant, not only a broken rule.

application.title: Winning can still be losing
application.body: A believer can win the case and still lose. Many family fights over money, inheritance or business deals are like this. Absorbing a loss sometimes protects something far more valuable than the money.
application.question: What dispute are you determined to win that may cost more than it gains?

application.title: Allowed, and still in charge
application.body: Something can be permitted and still own you. Phones, shopping, food and entertainment begin as freedoms and can end as masters. Paul's test is not only "Is it allowed?" but "Is it mastering me?"
application.question: What permitted thing do you reach for automatically when you are bored or anxious?

application.title: Run, do not negotiate
application.body: Paul does not tell believers to debate sexual temptation but to flee it. Joseph ran from Potiphar's wife and left his cloak behind (Genesis 39:12). Distance and practical barriers are not weakness; they are wisdom.
application.question: Where are you still negotiating with a temptation you should be running from?

context.heading: Quoting their letter back
context.body: "Now for the matters you wrote about" begins Paul's answers to a letter from Corinth. Many scholars think "It is good for a man not to touch a woman" was the Corinthians' own slogan. Haptō ("to touch") was a polite Greek idiom for sexual relations. Some ascetic believers apparently wanted even married couples to abstain, and Paul qualifies the slogan at once.

context.heading: "The present crisis"
context.body: Anankē means "necessity" or "distress". Paul's advice to stay as you are is tied to this crisis, and scholars are unsure what it was. Suggestions include the general pressure of the last days, persecution, or a local hardship such as the grain shortages known from this period. That setting matters when reading his cautions about marriage.

context.heading: The scenery is being changed
context.body: Schēma means "form" or "outward shape", and it could describe a role or scene in the theater. "This world in its present form is passing away" may picture stage scenery being changed between acts. Marriage, grief, joy, buying and selling are real and good, but they belong to a stage that will not last.

theology.title: God's call outranks status
theology.body: Paul repeats one principle three times: remain in the situation in which God called you (vv. 17, 20, 24). Circumcised or not, slave or free, married or single, none of these changes your standing before God. Yet Paul also urges a slave to gain freedom if possible (v. 21). God meets people where they are and gives every station dignity.

theology.title: Faithfulness in marriage
theology.body: Paul passes on Jesus' own command that married couples should not separate (v. 10; Mark 10:9). Lifelong marriage mirrors God's covenant faithfulness to His people. Paul then addresses a case Jesus did not, a believer whose unbelieving spouse leaves (v. 15). Faithful Christians differ on whether that permits remarriage, so these verses deserve careful study.

application.title: Mutual, not one-sided
application.body: Paul says husband and wife each have authority over the other's body, a startlingly mutual claim in a culture where husbands held most of the power. Withholding affection as leverage or through neglect is not neutral. Marriage is a place of giving, not keeping score.
application.question: Where are you treating part of your marriage, present or future, as yours alone to control?

application.title: Singleness is not a waiting room
application.body: Paul, apparently unmarried himself, calls singleness a gift that frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord. Churches can treat single adults as unfinished projects. The single years can be a season of focus, not just a delay.
application.question: How do you, or your church, treat single adults as if their real lives have not started yet?

application.title: Hold things loosely
application.body: Buy as if you did not own, and use the world without depending on it. Paul is not banning shopping; he is loosening your grip. A house, a job title or a bank balance is scenery on a stage that is already changing.
application.question: Which possession would truly shake your sense of security if it disappeared tomorrow?

context.heading: Dinner in the idol's temple
context.body: An eidōleion ("idol's temple") often had dining rooms where guests reclined for banquets, birthdays and trade-guild meals. Archaeologists have found such rooms at the sanctuary of Asclepius in Corinth. Turning down invitations could cost business and friendships. Paul notes the irony: the weak believer who sees you there will be "encouraged", literally "built up" (oikodomeō), to sin.

context.heading: Conscience as an inner witness
context.body: Syneidēsis ("conscience") literally means "knowing with", an inner awareness that sits in judgment on what you do. A "weak" conscience is not a wicked one. It belongs to someone whose old habits of idol worship still shape how they feel about the food. Pushing them to act against it, even toward a true conclusion, defiles them.

context.heading: A right that trips others
context.body: Proskomma is an obstacle you strike your foot against. For "freedom" Paul uses exousia, "right" or "authority", a key word in chapters 8–10. The strong were correct that idols are nothing. But a right used without love can become the rock that brings a brother down.

theology.title: The Creator died for the weak
theology.body: Verse 6 says all things come from the Father and exist through the Lord Jesus Christ. Jesus is not only Savior but the agent of creation, as John 1:3 and Colossians 1:16 also teach. The One who made everything is the One who died for the weak brother (v. 11). Creator and Redeemer are the same Lord.

theology.title: Known by God
theology.body: Paul shifts from knowing to being known: "the one who loves God is known by God" (v. 3). In Scripture God's knowing often means His choosing, covenant love (Amos 3:2; Galatians 4:9). Our grasp of truth is always partial, but His knowledge of His people is complete. That is firmer ground than our cleverness.

application.title: Right, and still wrong
application.body: You can win the argument and lose the person. Online debates, small-group theology fights and family disagreements all tempt us to prove a point instead of building someone up.
application.question: Who have you been right at lately rather than loving toward?

application.title: Your freedom has an audience
application.body: A drink at dinner, a film choice or how you spend Sunday may be fine for you and still affect someone newer in faith who is watching. Love sometimes means quietly setting a right aside. That is not legalism; it is choosing a person over a preference.
application.question: Which of your freedoms would you give up if you learned it was hurting someone's faith?

application.title: Handle tender consciences gently
application.body: Some believers come from backgrounds that make certain things feel dangerous to them. Mocking those scruples is easy and destructive. Help them grow, but do not shove them past what they can do in good faith.
application.question: Whose convictions do you dismiss as immature, and how could you serve that person instead?

context.heading: An ox on the threshing floor
context.body: Paul quotes Deuteronomy 25:4, which forbade muzzling an ox while it trampled grain, so it could eat as it worked. Jewish teachers often argued from lesser to greater, and Paul does the same: if God cares that an animal shares in its labor, how much more those who labor in the gospel. He reads the law for its deeper principle.

context.heading: A slave by choice
context.body: Douloō means "to enslave". In Corinth, where a large share of people were slaves or former slaves, the picture was vivid. Paul was free, by Acts' account a Roman citizen (Acts 22:28), and he chose a slave's posture toward everyone. Some status-minded Corinthians may have found his manual work degrading; he saw it as a strategy for reaching people.

context.heading: A boxer's black eye
context.body: Hypōpiazō literally means "to strike under the eye", to give a black eye. Paul pictures a boxer landing real blows rather than shadowboxing (v. 26), and the target is his own body. Adokimos ("disqualified") was used of an athlete or a coin that failed the test. Interpreters debate whether he fears losing salvation or losing his reward and usefulness.

theology.title: A God who provides for workers
theology.body: God built generosity into His law, from the ox at the threshing floor to the priests who ate from the altar (v. 13). Jesus commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should live by it (v. 14; Luke 10:7). God is not stingy with His servants, which makes Paul's choice to refuse pay all the more striking.

theology.title: Love that comes near
theology.body: Paul's flexibility mirrors Christ, who though rich became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9) and took the form of a slave (Philippians 2:7). In Jesus, God entered a particular culture, language and family to save people. Paul still stays "under the law of Christ" (v. 21). He adapts methods, never the message.

application.title: Give up a right on purpose
application.body: Paul did not merely tolerate losing his rights; he set them aside so nothing would block the gospel. Most of us defend our rights by reflex, at home, at work and online. A right freely surrendered can open doors that a right insisted on keeps shut.
application.question: Which right are you clinging to that may be getting in the way of someone hearing about Jesus?

application.title: Learn someone else's world
application.body: Becoming all things to all people takes effort: learning how a coworker, a teenager or an immigrant neighbor thinks and what matters to them. Paul did this without changing the message. Love does its homework.
application.question: Whose world have you never tried to understand because it felt foreign or uncomfortable?

application.title: Train instead of drifting
application.body: Isthmian athletes trained hard for a wreath that would wilt in days. Spiritual maturity also needs deliberate habits, like time in Scripture and saying no to the body's every demand. Drifting is the default; discipline is chosen.
application.question: What one habit would show that you are running to win rather than just jogging along?

context.heading: The rock that went with them
context.body: Israel received water from a rock near the start and the end of the wilderness years (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11). Later Jewish tradition told of a well or rock that traveled with Israel. Paul may be nodding to that idea, but his point is deeper: the true source of their provision was Christ Himself, present with Israel long before Bethlehem.

context.heading: Patterns stamped for us
context.body: Typos ("example") first meant the mark left by a blow, then a stamp, model or pattern, the root of our word "type". Israel's story is a pattern pressed into history for the church, "written down as warnings for us" (v. 11). Rescue and miraculous food did not protect Israel once they turned to idols.

context.heading: Demons behind the idols
context.body: Paul has said an idol is nothing (8:4), yet here pagan sacrifices are offered to daimonia ("demons"). He is echoing Deuteronomy 32:17, where Israel "sacrificed to demons, not to God". The statue is just stone, but real spiritual powers stand behind idolatry. That is why sharing in temple feasts is not neutral.

theology.title: Christ in Israel's story
theology.body: Paul reads the wilderness journey as the church's family history: the cloud and sea as a kind of baptism, the manna and water as spiritual food and drink, the rock as Christ. Calling Christ the rock echoes a title for God Himself (Deuteronomy 32:4). The same God who rescued Israel rescues us.

theology.title: Jealous and faithful
theology.body: "Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?" (v. 22) echoes Deuteronomy 32:21. God's jealousy is not insecurity; it is the rightful claim of a husband who will not share His bride with idols. The same God is faithful, limiting every test and providing a way out (v. 13). His holiness and His kindness belong together.

application.title: Privilege is not protection
application.body: Israel had the sea, the manna and the rock, and still fell. Growing up in church, knowing the Bible or serving in ministry does not make you immune. The warning is aimed at the one who is sure he stands firm.
application.question: Where does your spiritual track record make you feel safe from a fall you could actually take?

application.title: Find the exit early
application.body: God provides a way out, but it usually appears early, before the second click, the third drink or the angry text. The way of escape is often a dull practical step taken in time. Wait until you are deep in temptation and the door is much harder to see.
application.question: What is the earliest exit point in the temptation you face most often?

application.title: Even lunch can glorify God
application.body: Paul says even eating and drinking can be done for God's glory. That reaches into ordinary meals, spreadsheets and grocery runs. The question is not only what is allowed but what helps others and honors Him.
application.question: What ordinary part of your day have you never thought of as something to do for God's glory?

context.heading: Head: authority, source or both?
context.body: Kephalē ("head") is the hinge of verses 3–16, and its meaning is debated. Many scholars argue it means authority; others argue for source or origin, like the head of a river; some see both. The answer shapes how Christians apply the passage to men and women today. Either way, Paul grounds it in relationships, including Christ's relationship to God.

context.heading: Covered heads and public honor
context.body: In the Greco-Roman world a married woman's covered head often signaled modesty and her status as a wife. Roman men, by contrast, sometimes covered their heads when leading pagan sacrifices, which may explain Paul's word to men. Customs varied by place, so scholars reconstruct the setting differently, and churches today apply the passage in different ways.

context.heading: Whose supper is it?
context.body: Kyriakos ("the Lord's") means "belonging to the Lord", and Paul sets it against each person's own private meal (v. 21). Roman hosts often served better food to guests of higher rank, a habit writers like Pliny the Younger criticized. The Corinthians seem to have carried that ranking to the table of Christ, where the poor went hungry.

theology.title: The new covenant in His blood
theology.body: Jesus calls the cup "the new covenant in My blood" (v. 25), fulfilling Jeremiah 31:31–34 and echoing the covenant blood at Sinai (Exodus 24:8). God binds Himself to His people with a promise sealed by His own Son's death. The Supper is a covenant meal, a repeated sign that God keeps His word.

theology.title: Remembering that takes part
theology.body: "Do this in remembrance [anamnēsis] of Me" (v. 24) recalls Passover, a memorial through which each generation said "the Lord brought me out" (Exodus 12:14; 13:8). Remembering in Scripture means more than recalling facts. Christians differ on how Christ is present at the Supper, but all agree it proclaims His death until He comes.

theology.title: Mutual dependence before God
theology.body: Paul balances his argument: in the Lord, woman is not independent of man nor man of woman, and everything comes from God (vv. 11–12). Whatever readers conclude about roles, the chapter does not teach that either sex is of lesser worth to God.

application.title: Notice who eats last
application.body: In Corinth the hungry were likely those who arrived late after long workdays. Churches can still sort people by income, polish or social circle without noticing. Paul treats that as despising the church of God.
application.question: Who tends to be left on the edges when your church gathers, and what would it take to draw them in?

application.title: Examine how you treat the body
application.body: Paul's call to examine yourself before the Supper is tied to how you treat fellow believers, not only to private sins. Coming to the table while holding contempt for another member is exactly what he warns against. Reconciliation is part of preparation.
application.question: Is there anyone in your church you would rather not sit beside at the Lord's table?

application.title: Worship is not a stage
application.body: Whatever your view of head coverings, Paul's concern is that worship not shame others or dishonor God. What you wear, say or post can pull attention toward yourself in a setting meant to honor Christ.
application.question: When you serve or worship in public, whose attention are you hoping to get?

context.heading: Led to voiceless idols
context.body: Aphōnos means "voiceless" or "mute". In their pagan past the Corinthians were "led astray" to idols that could not speak, perhaps swept along by the excitement some cults encouraged. Paul contrasts that with the living Spirit who moves people to confess Christ. Intense spiritual experience proves nothing by itself; what it says about Jesus does.

context.heading: Cursed or Lord: the Spirit's test
context.body: Anathema meant something devoted to God for destruction, hence "cursed". It is unclear why anyone would say "Jesus be cursed": perhaps in uncontrolled speech, under pressure from opponents, or as a hypothetical. Paul's test is simple. The Spirit leads people to confess "Jesus is Lord", a costly claim where Caesar was hailed as lord.

context.heading: Gifts handed out, not ranked
context.body: Diairesis means "distribution" or "apportioning", and Paul uses it three times in verses 4–6: gifts from the same Spirit, service for the same Lord, workings from the same God. The variety is deliberate, assigned by God rather than earned. Verse 11 adds that the Spirit gives to each one "as He determines".

theology.title: The Trinity at work
theology.body: Verses 4–6 move from Spirit to Lord to God, an early Trinitarian pattern in the New Testament. The one God is the source of every gift, every kind of service and every result. The church's unity reflects the unity of God Himself, with real distinction and no division.

theology.title: God honors the overlooked
theology.body: Paul says God arranged the body to give greater honor to the parts that lacked it (v. 24). This is the God who chose the weak in chapter 1 and who lifts the lowly throughout Scripture (1 Samuel 2:7–8; Luke 1:52). In His church the overlooked are not tolerated extras; they are indispensable.

application.title: Stop comparing body parts
application.body: Some feel useless because their gift is quiet; others feel superior because theirs is visible. Paul calls both absurd. An ear wishing it were an eye does not make the body work better.
application.question: Whose gift do you envy, and what does that envy reveal about how you see your own?

application.title: The people you quietly rank lower
application.body: The parts that seem weaker are indispensable. In many churches that means the elderly widow who prays, the member with a disability, the volunteer who fixes the plumbing. Treat them as necessary, not as charity cases.
application.question: Who in your church have you quietly ranked as less important?

application.title: Hurt together, rejoice together
application.body: If one part suffers, every part suffers with it. That means showing up when another member's health, marriage or job collapses, and truly celebrating when someone gets the promotion you wanted. Both are harder than they sound.
application.question: Whose success would be hardest for you to celebrate right now?

context.heading: Corinthian brass making noise
context.body: Chalkos means "bronze", so the "ringing gong" is literally echoing bronze. Some think Paul has in mind bronze sound vessels used in theaters, while the kymbalon ("cymbal") was heard in the loud worship of pagan cults. Corinth was famous for its bronze work. Gifted speech without love, Paul says, is just more noise.

context.heading: No ledger of wrongs
context.body: Logizomai is an accounting word: to reckon, calculate or credit to an account. Love "keeps no account of wrongs"; it does not maintain a running ledger of other people's offenses. Paul uses the same verb for God crediting righteousness and not counting sin (Romans 4:3–8). Love treats others the way God has treated us.

context.heading: When the perfect comes
context.body: Teleios means "complete", "mature" or "perfect", from telos, "goal". Christians debate what "the perfect" refers to. Most interpreters think it means Christ's return, when we will see "face to face" (v. 12). Others argue it means the completed New Testament or a mature church, which shapes views on whether gifts like prophecy and tongues continue today.

theology.title: Love looks like God
theology.body: Paul describes love by what it does, and each line fits God's own character: patient and kind (Exodus 34:6), not keeping account of wrongs. "God is love" (1 John 4:8). The chapter is also a portrait of Jesus, who bore all things and endured the cross. To learn love is to learn God.

theology.title: Fully known, one day knowing fully
theology.body: "Then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known" (v. 12). God already knows His people completely, and the hope of the gospel is to see Him face to face, as Moses spoke with God (Numbers 12:8). Gifts belong to this age and will pass, but love lasts, because it is the life of God Himself.

application.title: Gifted and unbearable
application.body: Talent, knowledge and even sacrifice can be offered without love, and Paul says the total is nothing. A brilliant musician who belittles volunteers, or a generous giver who controls through money, is still a clanging cymbal. Skill amplifies who you are; it never replaces love.
application.question: Where are your gifts impressive but your love for the people nearest you thin?

application.title: Close the file
application.body: Many of us keep a mental file of what a spouse, parent or coworker has done wrong, ready to open in the next argument. Love closes that file. Forgiveness does not erase memory, but it stops using the past as ammunition.
application.question: What old offense are you keeping in reserve for the next argument?

application.title: Read the list with your name
application.body: Try reading Paul's description with your own name in place of "love". It becomes humbling within a line or two. Then read it with Jesus' name, and see both the love you need and the love you have been shown.
application.question: Which line of the list would your family say describes you least?

context.heading: A trumpet no one can read
context.body: The salpinx ("trumpet") signaled soldiers to advance, retreat or form ranks. If it gave an adēlos ("unclear") sound, the army would not know what to do. Paul's point is that worship must communicate. Sound without meaning, however impressive, leaves the church unprepared.

context.heading: The outsider in the room
context.body: Idiōtēs ("uninstructed") meant a private person or layman without specialized training. It is the root of our word "idiot", though without the insult. Here it seems to describe an inquirer or newcomer in the meeting. Paul wants that person to understand enough to say "Amen", the Hebrew word of agreement used in synagogue prayer.

context.heading: Mistaken for a frenzied cult
context.body: Mainomai means "to rave" or "to be mad". Greeks linked ecstatic, uncontrolled speech with cults like that of Dionysus, whose worshipers were known for frenzy. A visitor walking into a meeting where everyone spoke in tongues at once would assume the same. Paul wants worship that points people to God, not to confusion.

theology.title: God speaks to be understood
theology.body: From Sinai to the prophets to Jesus, God speaks so His people can understand and respond (Deuteronomy 30:11–14; Hebrews 1:1–2). Prophecy here exposes hearts so that an outsider falls down and declares, "God is truly among you!" (v. 25), echoing Isaiah 45:14. God reveals Himself in order to be known and worshiped.

theology.title: Freedom and order from one God
theology.body: Paul expects many people to contribute a psalm, a teaching or a revelation (v. 26), yet he grounds order in God's character as a God of peace. Christians read the instructions to women in verses 34–35 in different ways, especially since Paul assumes women pray and prophesy in 11:5. All agree the goal is worship that builds up.

application.title: Serve the room, not your image
application.body: Paul's test for any contribution is whether it builds others up. A comment in small group, a prayer or a song choice can serve the room or serve your image. The difference is often who you are thinking about while you speak.
application.question: When you speak up at church, who are you mostly thinking about?

application.title: Picture the first-time visitor
application.body: Paul imagines an outsider walking in and asks how the gathering looks to them. Insider jargon, unexplained rituals and private jokes can lock people out without anyone meaning to. Hospitality includes being understandable.
application.question: What would a first-time visitor find confusing about the way you talk about your faith?

application.title: Grow up in your thinking
application.body: Paul tells the Corinthians to stop thinking like children: be infants in evil but mature in understanding. Faith that refuses to think is not humility; it is underdevelopment.
application.question: What question about your faith have you avoided thinking through because it felt easier not to?

context.heading: An untimely birth
context.body: Ektrōma means a premature or stillborn birth. Paul may be borrowing an insult his opponents used, or describing how abruptly and late he was brought to life as an apostle. Either way he calls himself the least of the apostles, because he persecuted the church. His calling is pure grace (v. 10).

context.heading: Baptized for the dead
context.body: Verse 29 mentions people "baptized for the dead", one of the most puzzling lines in the New Testament, with dozens of proposed explanations. Paul neither explains nor endorses the practice. He simply notes that it makes no sense if the dead are not raised. Firm conclusions here are best held loosely.

context.heading: A Spirit-filled body, not a ghost
context.body: Pneumatikos ("spiritual") does not mean made of spirit. In 2:15 the same word describes a person led by the Spirit. A "spiritual body" is a real body fully animated by God's Spirit, as a psychikos ("natural") body is animated by ordinary life. The risen Jesus ate and could be touched (Luke 24:39–43).

theology.title: The last Adam
theology.body: Death came through one man, and resurrection comes through another (vv. 21–22). Paul calls Christ "the last Adam" (v. 45), head of a new humanity as Adam was of the old. God has not abandoned His good creation. He is restoring it and raising it to glory, from dust to the image of the man from heaven.

theology.title: Death loses its sting
theology.body: Paul quotes Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 to taunt death. Kentron ("sting") was a scorpion's stinger or a cattle goad; sin gives death its poison, and the law gives sin its power (v. 56). Christ took that sting on Himself. God does not merely comfort His people in death; He defeats it.

theology.title: God all in all
theology.body: History ends with the Son handing the kingdom to the Father after destroying every enemy, death last, so that God may be all in all (vv. 24–28). This describes the Son's role in God's saving plan, not a lesser nature. The story is heading toward God's complete, unopposed reign.

application.title: A faith you can examine
application.body: Paul pointed to named witnesses, most still alive, who could be questioned. Christian faith is not a private feeling but a claim about something that happened. Doubts can be brought to the evidence instead of hushed.
application.question: Have you ever actually examined the evidence for the resurrection, or only assumed it?

application.title: Bad company, real effects
application.body: Paul quotes a Greek playwright: "Bad company corrupts good character." Some Corinthians had absorbed the denial of the resurrection from the people around them. The voices you listen to most shape what you are able to believe.
application.question: Whose voice in your feed or friendships is quietly reshaping what you believe?

application.title: Not one ounce wasted
application.body: Paul ends the great resurrection chapter with something practical: keep working, because your labor in the Lord is not in vain. If bodies will be raised, what you do with your body, time and work today carries forward. Changing diapers and doing honest work are not wasted.
application.question: What work in your life feels most pointless, and how does the resurrection change that?

context.heading: A collection, not a tax
context.body: Logeia ("collection") appears in Greek papyri for money gathered for a temple or as a levy. Paul's collection was voluntary and for poor believers in Jerusalem. It mattered to him as a sign that Gentile churches and Jewish believers were one family (Romans 15:25–27). Steady weekly giving meant no last-minute pressure when he arrived.

context.heading: An open door and many opponents
context.body: Thyra ("door") was a common image for opportunity. Paul stays in Ephesus because a great door for effective work has opened, even though many oppose him. He sees no contradiction between the two. Acts 19 describes this period in Ephesus, including the riot over the goddess Artemis.

context.heading: The church in their house
context.body: Aquila and Prisca (Priscilla) were tentmakers who worked with Paul in Corinth after being expelled from Rome (Acts 18:2–3). Now in Ephesus they host a church in their home. Early Christians had no church buildings; they met in households, which shaped how the Corinthians ate, prayed and argued together.

theology.title: One family across borders
theology.body: The collection shows the gospel's reach: Gentile believers in Greece giving to Jewish believers in Judea. God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3), and now that blessing flows back toward Jerusalem. Money becomes a sign of one people in Christ.

theology.title: Love has the last word
theology.body: After sixteen chapters of correction, Paul says "Do everything in love" (v. 14) and signs off with "My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus" (v. 24). The God who corrected this church through Paul did so in love. Even His hardest words aim at a people made whole.

application.title: Give on a rhythm
application.body: Paul asks for regular, proportional giving, set aside on the first day of each week. Generosity that waits for leftover money rarely happens. A plan decided in advance protects giving from mood and impulse.
application.question: What would change if you decided your giving before the month started instead of at its end?

application.title: Opposition is not a closed door
application.body: Paul stayed where he faced opposition because the door was open. Many of us read every difficulty as God's signal to quit. Resistance can mean you are exactly where the work is.
application.question: Which hard situation have you treated as a sign to leave when it may be the place to stay?

application.title: Name the people who refresh you
application.body: Paul names Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, who devoted themselves to serving and refreshed his spirit. Churches run on people like them, and Paul tells the church to show its appreciation.
application.question: Who has refreshed your spirit recently that you have never thanked by name?
